paragraphs: The paper studies how to turn a source-code snippet into a very short description resembling a function name. Producing such a summary requires selecting a few informative pieces from an input whose length can vary. The authors focus on improving the attention mechanism that guides this selection, particularly its ability to recognize useful patterns wherever they occur in the input.

Their network applies convolution to code tokens to identify local patterns and broader topical signals in a context-dependent way. It generates the summary one token at a time using two attention mechanisms. One predicts a summary token from the attended input, while the other can copy an existing code token directly. The model combines these possibilities by marginalizing over the mechanisms.

On ten popular Java projects, the proposed network performs better than previous attention mechanisms. The result supports using convolutional features to guide attention in this summarization setting. The copying mechanism also gives the architecture an explicit way to preserve an informative token already present in the code.
icml-2016-a-convolutional-attention-netw.tldr: A convolutional attention network generates short code summaries by combining token prediction with direct copying, improving results on ten Java projects.

paragraphs: Many graph learning problems begin with a small set of seed vertices and ask for a nearby region that is well separated from the rest of the graph. The paper introduces SimpleLocal, a method that uses minimum-cut and maximum-flow ideas to find cuts with good conductance near those seeds. Conductance provides the criterion for judging how well the selected region separates from its surroundings.

The central property is strong locality: SimpleLocal can find locally optimal cuts without exploring the entire graph. This matters when the graph is large but the desired region occupies only part of it. The method is related to earlier local flow algorithms, while allowing a simple implementation. The analysis also explains its localization through an implicit l1 penalty.

The authors report advantages in cut optimality and accurate recovery of target regions. They demonstrate the method on segmentation problems using an MRI-derived graph containing 467 million edges. This application illustrates the practical value of focusing computation near seeds; the optimality claim concerns local cuts.
icml-2016-a-simple-and-strongly-local-fl.tldr: SimpleLocal finds locally optimal graph cuts near seed vertices without needing to explore the entire graph.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to give a recurrent neural network more memory without increasing its number of learned parameters. Its proposed memory is associative, meaning that the system stores information in a form designed to support later retrieval. The construction uses complex-valued vectors and connects ideas from Long Short-Term Memory networks with Holographic Reduced Representations.

A difficulty with Holographic Reduced Representations is interference. As more information is stored, the stored contents increasingly interfere with one another, making retrieval noisier. The proposed system creates redundant copies of the information. This redundancy enables retrieval with reduced noise, addressing a specific obstacle to using the associative store as additional network memory.

Experiments show faster learning on multiple memorization tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the memory construction for the tested tasks, particularly where retaining and retrieving information is central. The contribution separates additional memory from additional learned parameters: the network gains a way to store information without expanding its parameter count.
icml-2016-associative-long-short-term-me.tldr: An associative memory augments recurrent networks without adding parameters, using redundant storage to reduce retrieval noise and accelerate learning on memorization tasks.

paragraphs: The paper presents a lightweight framework for training neural networks to control an agent through reinforcement learning. Its organizing idea is asynchronous gradient descent with multiple actor-learners working in parallel. The authors build asynchronous versions of four standard reinforcement learning algorithms, showing how the same general training framework can support several learning methods.

Parallel actor-learners have a stabilizing effect in the reported experiments, allowing all four methods to train neural network controllers successfully. This makes the parallelism relevant to learning behavior as well as computation. The strongest method is an asynchronous actor-critic variant, which combines learning how to act with learning to evaluate the outcomes of actions.

On Atari, that method exceeds the state of the art reported in the paper while taking half the training time on a single multicore CPU instead of a GPU. It also succeeds on varied continuous motor-control problems and on navigating random three-dimensional mazes from visual input. Together, these results demonstrate applicability across several distinct control settings.
icml-2016-asynchronous-methods-for-deep-.tldr: Parallel asynchronous actor-learners stabilize deep reinforcement learning, with actor-critic delivering strong results across Atari, motor control, and visual maze navigation.

paragraphs: The paper extends Barron and Cover’s theory to general supervised learning without the approximation required by its original application in this setting. Earlier developments had removed approximation in other formulations, but their approach did not generally carry over to supervised learning. The authors address this obstacle by developing an extension suited to that setting.

The extended theory retains several useful properties: it applies at finite sample sizes, requires few assumptions, and justifies the minimum description length principle in supervised learning. That principle connects model selection with describing the data and model compactly. A finite-sample result matters because its statement applies to a particular amount of observed data, rather than relying only on behavior as the sample grows.

As an application, the authors derive new risk and regret bounds for lasso with random design. The risk bound holds for any finite sample size without requiring bounded features. They also examine the regret bound numerically. These contributions provide theoretical guarantees for lasso, with simulations investigating how one of those guarantees behaves.
icml-2016-barron-and-covers-theory-in-su.tldr: An extension of Barron and Cover’s theory yields finite-sample supervised-learning guarantees and new lasso bounds without requiring bounded features.

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual bandits, where a learner uses contextual information to select an action and learns from the reward of that choice. Its main setting assumes independently and identically distributed contexts, while allowing an arbitrary reward sequence and an arbitrary policy class. BISTRO addresses the computational problem of learning under these conditions.

On each round, BISTRO makes one call to an empirical risk minimization oracle for each available action. It uses unlabeled data to simplify the computation. When exact empirical risk minimization is itself difficult, the authors extend the approach to multiplicative approximation algorithms. The relaxation’s integrality gap affects the regret bound while leaving the comparison benchmark unchanged.

The paper also gives a conditional result for adversarial contextual bandits. Learnability follows whenever the corresponding full-information supervised online learning problem has a nontrivial regret bound, with efficiency when that problem is efficient. This connects learning from limited action feedback to a fuller-feedback problem and identifies a condition under which the harder feedback setting remains manageable.
icml-2016-bistro-an-efficient-relaxation.tldr: BISTRO uses unlabeled data and empirical risk minimization oracles to make contextual bandit learning computationally tractable under stated conditions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses link prediction in knowledge bases: estimating which relationships hold between entities. It uses latent factorization, representing relational structure through learned embeddings. Its distinguishing choice is to use complex-valued embeddings, giving the model a way to express a broad range of binary relationships within a relatively simple mathematical construction.

The composition of these embeddings can represent both symmetric and antisymmetric relations. This distinction matters because some relationships behave the same way when the two entities exchange positions, while others depend on their order. The scoring construction uses the Hermitian dot product, a counterpart of the ordinary dot product for complex vectors. The authors describe it as arguably simpler than Neural Tensor Networks and Holographic Embeddings.

The approach retains linear space and time requirements, supporting its use with large datasets. On standard link-prediction benchmarks, it consistently outperforms the alternative approaches evaluated. The findings show that complex-valued representations can provide useful relational expressiveness while keeping the model’s core operation simple and its computational requirements scalable.
icml-2016-complex-embeddings-for-simple-.tldr: Complex-valued embeddings model varied relation types with a simple Hermitian dot product and outperform alternatives on standard link-prediction benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies statistical hypothesis testing when the sample contains sensitive information about individuals. A hypothesis test uses observations to decide whether a proposed model should be rejected. The authors place this task under differential privacy, making protection of the people represented in the sample part of the statistical problem.

The first focus is chi-squared goodness-of-fit testing for multinomial data. Here, the observations belong to categories, and the question concerns whether their observed distribution is compatible with a proposed model. The second focus is testing independence between two categorical variables. This asks whether their observed relationship provides grounds to reject an independence assumption.

These two settings concern different statistical judgments, but both require drawing conclusions from data that may include private individual records. The paper’s contribution, as described in the abstract, is its study of these chi-squared testing problems subject to differential privacy. Its motivation is to make privacy guarantees part of hypothesis testing, including applications where the underlying observations contain sensitive medical information.
icml-2016-differentially-private-chi-squ.tldr: The paper studies differentially private chi-squared tests for categorical goodness of fit and independence.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a neural network architecture for model-free reinforcement learning. It separates two quantities that are useful when assessing actions: the value of the current state and the advantage of an action in that state. This gives the network distinct estimators for how favorable the situation is and how individual actions compare within it.

The purpose of this factoring is to let learning generalize across actions. Information about the value of a state can contribute to evaluating several actions, while the advantage estimator captures their differences. The architecture can provide this separation without requiring a change to the underlying reinforcement learning algorithm, making it an architectural contribution to how values are represented.

The reported results show better policy evaluation when many actions have similar values. That finding fits the motivation for separately representing what actions share and how they differ. The resulting agent also exceeds the state of the art reported for Atari 2600, demonstrating that the architectural change improves performance in that evaluated domain.
icml-2016-dueling-network-architectures-.tldr: Dueling networks separate state value from action advantage, improving evaluation with similar-valued actions and achieving stronger Atari results.

paragraphs: The paper asks how convolutional networks can use rotational symmetry in images more directly. Training with rotated examples exposes a network to different orientations, but still leaves it to learn how its representations should respond to rotation. The authors investigate encoding some of that behavior into the architecture, much as convolution encodes a relationship between input translations and feature responses.

They introduce four operations that can be inserted as network layers. Combining these operations produces models that are partially equivariant to rotations, meaning that some internal responses change in a structured way when the input rotates. The operations also allow parameters to be shared across orientations, providing a way to reuse learned features.

The authors evaluate these architectural changes on three datasets exhibiting rotational symmetry and report improved performance with smaller models. This supports their proposal that building appropriate symmetry into a network can make more efficient use of its parameters. The stated construction provides partial rotation equivariance, and the empirical benefits are demonstrated on the evaluated datasets.
icml-2016-exploiting-cyclic-symmetry-in-.tldr: Four layer operations build partial rotation equivariance and orientation-based parameter sharing into networks, improving performance with smaller models on three datasets.

paragraphs: The Nyström method makes kernel methods more scalable by using selected landmarks to construct an approximation. Its effectiveness depends strongly on which landmarks are chosen. This paper studies selection through determinantal point processes, or DPPs, probability models that favor diverse samples. Diversity provides a principled basis for choosing the points used in the approximation.

The authors prove approximation-error bounds for DPP-selected landmarks and analyze what those bounds imply for kernel ridge regression. They also address a computational concern: DPP sampling had been associated with cubic cost. Under certain conditions, they show that a Markov chain sampling approach instead requires time linear in the size of the dataset.

Empirical results support the theoretical analysis and show better performance for DPP landmark selection than the existing approaches considered. The contribution therefore addresses both the quality of the approximation and the cost of obtaining its landmarks. The linear-time sampling result is conditional, so its significance is that efficient sampling is available in the settings covered by the analysis.
icml-2016-fast-dpp-sampling-for-nystrom-.tldr: DPP landmark selection provides Nyström approximation guarantees, with linear-time Markov chain sampling under certain conditions and strong empirical results.

paragraphs: This paper develops a methodology and tools for examining what Deep Q-networks (DQNs) learn in reinforcement learning. Its aim is to make their internal representations and learned behavior understandable. This matters because assessing a network’s success leaves open the question of how its learned features organize the situations it encounters.

The authors report that DQN features group the state space hierarchically. In plain language, the learned representation brings states together in a layered organization. They present this structure as an explanation for DQNs’ success, connecting the organization inside the network with its ability to learn useful behavior.

The tools also let the authors understand and describe the policies learned for three Atari2600 games: how the networks choose actions in those settings. These analyses connect internal features with behavior that can be interpreted. Building on that work, the authors suggest ways to interpret, debug, and optimize deep neural networks in reinforcement learning. Those suggestions point toward practical uses for the analysis tools; the abstract’s concrete findings concern the hierarchical representations and the policies examined in those three games.
icml-2016-graying-the-black-box-understa.tldr: The paper introduces tools that reveal hierarchical state grouping in DQNs and help explain their learned policies across three Atari2600 games.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the cost of multiplying a tall data matrix by a Gaussian random matrix. It constructs a different randomized transform whose output distribution can be made arbitrarily close, in total variation distance, to the output of the Gaussian multiplication. The objective is to preserve the probabilistic usefulness of the original operation while reducing computation.

For an n-by-d input X and an m-by-n transform, the stated runtime is O(nnz(X)) plus a term of order m^1.5 times d^3 with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here nnz(X) counts nonzero entries. This improves substantially on the direct O(nnz(X) times m) computation when the input’s nonzero count is much larger than m^1.5 times d^3.

The distributional guarantee makes the replacement broadly useful: applications can retain the Gaussian transform’s guarantees up to a small additive change in error probability. Thus, the result concerns downstream probabilistic guarantees as well as speed. The authors apply the transform to nonnegative matrix factorization and support vector machines, illustrating two uses of the construction.
icml-2016-how-to-fake-multiply-by-a-gaus.tldr: A randomized transform approximates Gaussian matrix multiplication in distribution, offering substantial speedups under a stated size condition.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a practical difficulty in clustering: a grouping suggested by the data may not match the user’s needs. It focuses on hierarchical clustering, where groups are organized at multiple levels. The authors seek a way for user feedback to shape this hierarchy while retaining information about the geometry of the data.

Their algorithm takes a Bayesian approach, sampling from a posterior distribution over hierarchies subject to constraints obtained through interaction. This combines user-provided requirements with the structure supported by the observations. Representing possible hierarchies through a constrained posterior gives the interaction a role within the clustering procedure itself.

The authors also propose several strategies for choosing questions to ask the user. This makes query selection a second part of the approach, alongside incorporating the answers into clustering. The algorithm and querying schemes show promising results on real data. Those findings support the feasibility of interactive hierarchical clustering that responds to user needs while continuing to use the data’s geometric organization.
icml-2016-interactive-bayesian-hierarchi.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchical clustering algorithm incorporates user constraints and proposes query strategies, with promising results on real data.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a framework for learning convolutional neural networks from graph data. It supports arbitrary graphs, including directed and undirected structures, and permits both discrete and continuous attributes on nodes and edges. This broad input scope lets the framework address graph learning problems with different kinds of connectivity and descriptive information.

The key step is extracting locally connected regions from a graph. This parallels the use of local image regions in image-based convolutional networks: the model learns from connected portions of its input. The paper provides a general approach for obtaining those regions from graphs, supplying the local inputs needed for convolutional feature learning.

On established benchmark datasets, the learned representations are competitive with state-of-the-art graph kernels and are highly efficient to compute. The reported outcome supports convolutional learning as a practical approach to graph representation. Its significance combines flexible graph inputs with efficient computation and competitive predictive representations, without claiming that the framework surpasses every graph-kernel alternative.
icml-2016-learning-convolutional-neural-.tldr: A framework extracts local graph regions for convolutional learning, producing efficient representations competitive with state-of-the-art graph kernels.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the share of one component in a mixture when samples are available from both the mixture and that component. This quantity is useful in weakly supervised learning, including learning from positive and unlabeled examples, handling label noise, anomaly detection, and crowdsourcing. The task is to recover a mixing weight from these samples.

The proposed method embeds probability distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, giving the estimation problem a kernel-based representation. Its implementation requires solving a simple convex quadratic program a few times. The authors prove correctness and derive convergence rates under certain assumptions on the distributions, connecting a computational procedure to guarantees about approaching the true proportion.

On several standard classification datasets, the algorithm performs comparably to or better than other methods on most datasets. These empirical results complement the conditional convergence theory. The contribution is an efficient estimation approach with proven rates in the covered setting, supported by comparisons showing that the method is practically competitive.
icml-2016-mixture-proportion-estimation-.tldr: Kernel embeddings yield an efficient mixture-proportion estimator with conditional convergence guarantees and competitive performance on classification datasets.

paragraphs: The paper introduces truncated Gaussian graphical models as a framework for nonlinear statistical learning. It begins with a Gaussian graphical model and constrains a subset of its variables to be nonnegative. These constrained variables are latent, so the model’s observable distribution is obtained by integrating them out rather than treating them as observed inputs.

This construction produces a marginal model whose variables are non-Gaussian and whose expected relationships are nonlinear. It therefore creates nonlinear behavior through a structured modification of a Gaussian model. The authors use expectation-maximization to express inference as a sequence of truncated Gaussian graphical-model problems, each solved efficiently with properties and numerical methods of multivariate Gaussian distributions.

The framework is used to construct models for both nonlinear regression and classification. The authors demonstrate their performance on extensive benchmark datasets and compare them with state-of-the-art competing results. The contribution connects nonlinear modeling to Gaussian computational tools, providing a common modeling and inference approach for these two kinds of prediction tasks.
icml-2016-nonlinear-statistical-learning.tldr: Truncating latent Gaussian variables creates nonlinear regression and classification models whose inference can use multivariate Gaussian methods.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis learns representations that reveal correlations between different views of the same data. Nonlinear versions often restrict the transformations through a chosen kernel or neural architecture and can be computationally demanding. This paper revisits population-level theory for unrestricted nonlinear CCA and turns it into a practical nonparametric algorithm.

The authors express the solution through a singular value decomposition of an operator associated with the views’ joint density. Estimating that density from data reduces the practical task to an eigenvalue problem without requiring inversion of a kernel matrix. They also introduce partially linear CCA, which applies a linear projection to one view and a nonparametric transformation to the other.

Using kernel density estimates based on a small number of nearest neighbors, the resulting algorithms are memory-efficient and often much faster than the compared approaches. They perform better than kernel CCA and comparably to deep CCA. These results show how the theoretical formulation can lead to useful representations with a favorable computational profile.
icml-2016-nonparametric-canonical-correl.tldr: Nonparametric CCA uses density estimation and an eigenvalue problem to learn correlated views without kernel-matrix inversion.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization when several objectives must be considered together and evaluating them is expensive. Bayesian optimization selects evaluations sequentially using a probabilistic model and decision theory. In the multi-objective setting, the relevant goal involves understanding tradeoffs among objectives, making relationships between their outcomes potentially useful to the search.

A common simplification is to model each objective independently, which makes computation easier. The authors instead incorporate correlations between objectives. This lets the model represent dependencies that independence would exclude. Accounting for those dependencies introduces intractable integrals, so the paper develops an approximation to make the resulting approach computationally manageable.

The authors illustrate the value of modeling objective dependencies on a range of synthetic and real-world multi-objective problems. These examples support treating correlation as useful information when learning about expensive objectives. The contribution brings dependence modeling into the Bayesian treatment of the problem and supplies an approximation for the computational difficulty it creates, with empirical evidence for its usefulness in the evaluated settings.
icml-2016-pareto-frontier-learning-with-.tldr: A Bayesian multi-objective optimization approach models correlations between expensive objectives and approximates the resulting intractable integrals.

paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical method for comparing persistence diagrams, descriptors used in topological data analysis to summarize shape-related structure. These diagrams help distinguish robust topological properties from noisy ones. The authors propose a kernel on persistence diagrams, providing a similarity construction that can support a statistical framework for this kind of information.

The kernel has a stability property and allows explicit control over the influence of persistence. These features address related concerns: making comparisons stable and controlling how strongly topological properties contribute according to their persistence. The method also admits a fast approximation technique, connecting its mathematical construction with a more computationally practical way to use it.

Applications to protein and oxide-glass data show advantages over other relevant methods on persistence diagrams. The findings demonstrate usefulness in the evaluated practical datasets. The contribution combines a stable comparison method, adjustable persistence effects, and fast approximation, giving statistical analysis a way to work with topological descriptors while retaining the significance of their persistence information.
icml-2016-persistence-weighted-gaussian-.tldr: A stable kernel compares persistence diagrams with explicit control over persistence effects and supports fast approximation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a GPU implementation technique for recurrent neural networks, focusing on high computational throughput at small minibatch sizes. Its key idea is to keep recurrent weights on-chip and reuse them across multiple time steps through persistent computational kernels. This uses the GPU’s memory hierarchy to improve how the recurrent computation is mapped onto hardware.

The initial implementation sustains 2.8 TFLOP/s with a minibatch size of four on an NVIDIA TitanX. The authors report substantially higher throughput at small minibatch sizes than direct implementations based on matrix multiplication. The result shows that the implementation strategy can make small-batch recurrent computation efficient on the evaluated hardware.

The paper reports a sixteenfold reduction in activation memory and the ability to train models with twelve times as many parameters on the same hardware. It also enables strong scaling to 128 GPUs and efficient exploration of end-to-end speech recognition models exceeding 100 layers. These outcomes connect weight reuse to practical gains in memory use, model capacity, and distributed training.
icml-2016-persistent-rnns-stashing-recur.tldr: Persistent GPU kernels reuse recurrent weights across time steps, improving small-batch throughput and enabling larger and deeper RNN training.

paragraphs: Rejection sampling generates samples from a difficult target distribution by proposing candidates and accepting only some of them. Its usefulness can be limited when too many proposals are rejected. The paper introduces pliable rejection sampling, or PRS, to improve the proposal through learning while retaining guarantees about the resulting sampling process.

PRS learns its sampling proposal using a kernel estimator. Adapting the proposal addresses the central efficiency issue: a proposal poorly suited to the target can waste many candidate draws. The authors position their approach against adaptive rejection methods that either apply only to very specific distributions or lack performance guarantees.

The stated results cover both sample validity and acceptance performance. With high probability, the obtained samples are independent, identically distributed, and drawn from the target distribution. PRS also provides a guarantee on the number of accepted samples. This combination matters because improving acceptance is useful only alongside control over what distribution the accepted samples represent; the validity claim retains its high-probability qualification.
icml-2016-pliable-rejection-sampling-d00.tldr: PRS learns a rejection-sampling proposal with a kernel estimator, providing high-probability sample validity and a guarantee on accepted sample counts.

paragraphs: The paper examines how recurrent neural networks retain information over long sequences. It focuses on two synthetic datasets used to evaluate long-term memory. Rather than relying only on observed training outcomes, the authors explicitly construct recurrent networks that solve these problems, making it possible to inspect how a successful solution stores the information it needs.

These constructions clarify both the demands of the tasks and the roles of information held in the hidden state. A hidden state carries information from one time step to the next, so understanding its contents is central to understanding long-memory behavior. The constructed solutions reveal how different kinds of information can be represented within that state.

The analysis also explains the success of recent methods using unitary initializations or constraints on transition matrices. Its contribution is therefore explanatory: concrete solutions help connect task structure, memory representation, and recurrent-network design. The findings concern the two analyzed synthetic problems and use their solutions to illuminate why those approaches can work well.
icml-2016-recurrent-orthogonal-networks-.tldr: Explicit RNN solutions to two long-memory tasks explain hidden-state storage and the success of unitary transition initializations or constraints.

paragraphs: The paper asks when a multivariate time series reveals whether it is being viewed forward or backward. It studies linear vector autoregressive moving-average models. The authors prove that when all innovations are normally distributed, reversing time preserves the same model assumption. Under the stated non-Gaussian innovation setting, this reversibility breaks down, making time direction detectable.

This result provides a theoretical basis for an existing approach to identifying the direction of video snippets. The authors present a slightly modified practical algorithm for estimating direction from a sample and prove its consistency. They also investigate how performance changes with sample size, the number of dimensions, and the order of the process.

An application to economic data shows that using multiple variables together can help estimate time direction compared with using a single variable. The work extends earlier univariate results and connects with causal-inference approaches that use non-Gaussian errors. Its central insight is conditional on the time-series model and noise assumptions: distributional structure can make temporal direction identifiable.
icml-2016-the-arrow-of-time-in-multivari.tldr: Under a VARMA model with non-Gaussian innovations, time direction becomes detectable, motivating a consistent estimation algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn expressive models while keeping inference computationally tractable. It generalizes the tractability of sum-product networks to problems whose inference can be expressed as summing a function over a semiring. This algebraic formulation covers several kinds of tasks, including satisfiability, constraint satisfaction, optimization, and integration.

The key theorem gives a sufficient condition: within every product, the factors must depend on disjoint sets of variables. Enforcing this structural condition during learning ensures tractability of the learned models in the framework. This unifies and extends earlier results by identifying a common way to control inference cost across otherwise different problems.

The authors demonstrate the approach by learning a nonconvex function that can nevertheless be globally optimized in polynomial time. Empirically, this greatly outperforms learning without accounting for optimization cost. The example shows why the condition matters for model design: the learned function can remain expressive while retaining a tractable route to its global optimum. Disjoint scopes are presented as sufficient, rather than necessary, for tractability.
icml-2016-the-sum-product-theorem-a-foun.tldr: A sufficient disjoint-scope condition guarantees tractable semiring inference and enables learning nonconvex functions that can be globally optimized in polynomial time.
